title: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
hook: Shalya keeps his promise with a story about a crow and a swan
carry: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
tomorrow: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karna took command and asked for Shalya at the reins, and Shalya came with a promise to the other side. Whose voice did you notice riding along with you? Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

What does a driver say as the chariot rolls out to battle? Karna is in high spirits. He calls out across the field: whoever shows me where Arjuna is, I'll reward him richly. And beside him, holding the reins, Shalya laughs. Save your gifts, he says, in effect. You'll see Arjuna soon enough, and you won't enjoy it. Karna boasts again. Shalya mocks again. Back and forth, two proud men in one small chariot, the army watching. Then Shalya stops arguing and does something sharper. He tells a story. Today, the story he tells, and who it's really about.
screen: `KARNA CALLS FOR ARJUNA.` → `SHALYA LAUGHS.` → `A STORY INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's English, Shalya's story goes like this. A crow lived in a merchant's house, and the merchant's children fed it the leftovers from their plates. Well fed, the crow grew proud. One day some swans came by, and the crow challenged them: I can fly better than any of you. I know more ways to fly than you can name. A swan answered simply: I know one way. Then they set out over the ocean. The crow showed off, diving and wheeling, every trick it knew. The swan flew straight. Far out over the water the crow grew tired. Its wings dragged. It sank toward the waves, with nowhere to land, and it begged the swan for help. And the swan lifted the exhausted crow onto its back and carried it back to land. Then Shalya turns to Karna. You, he says, are that crow, fed on the leftovers of Dhritarashtra's sons, and Arjuna is the swan. That's the promise to Yudhishthira, kept. Not with an arrow. With a fable, aimed at Karna's courage. Karna doesn't turn back. He answers with hard words of his own, and the chariot rolls on toward Arjuna. The story inside the story is small and almost gentle. The swan doesn't gloat. It just flies one way, straight, and when the boaster falls, it lifts him up.
screen: `THE CROW FED ON LEFTOVERS` · `I KNOW ONE WAY TO FLY` · `THE SWAN LIFTS THE CROW` · then, large: `YOU ARE THAT CROW`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath find one simple path: in through the nose, out slowly. No tricks, no diving and wheeling. Just one way. When your mind starts showing off, rehearsing, arguing, planning, notice it, and come back to the straight line of the breath. In, and out. If someone's words have been aimed at you lately, let them sit beside you without answering. If you pray, you can rest in prayer here. The bell holds the time.
Karna. The commander who rides out boasting, and hears his driver tell him he's the crow, and rides on anyway.
Your line: Karna, the wheel stuck, the death. Today, when you want to show off every trick you know, try one way, done straight. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Shalya's fable of the crow and the swan is retold in readings of the Karna Parva and in collections of Mahabharata stories, where it can travel on its own as a story about pride.

fork.setup: you're the swan, far out over the ocean. the crow who mocked you is sinking toward the waves, begging for help. what do you do?
options: lift it onto your back and carry it home.
circle and remind it of its boasting.
fork.reveal: the swan carries the crow back to land. the story's sting is for Karna, not the crow: Shalya says Karna is that crow.

original.note: swan: the bird in Shalya's story that flies one way, straight, and saves the crow.

trapdoor: what you thought: the crow and the swan is a simple fable for children.
what it means: Shalya aims it at Karna like an arrow: you are the crow, Arjuna is the swan.
what a scholar hears: the epic sets a story inside a story here, and the teller is supposed to be on Karna's side, which turns a fable into a weapon.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, Karna's boast and offer of rewards, Shalya's mockery, and Shalya's story of the crow and the swans

notes: Editor pass: replaced the count 'a hundred ways' (Ganguli's figure differs) with 'more ways than you can name', changed 'carried it home' to 'back to land', and removed 'often' claims from the trapdoor and howItsDone.

All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli the details of the fable: the crow fed on leavings by a merchant's (Vaishya's) children, its boast of many kinds of flight (the voice says 'a hundred ways' as the crow's own boast; check the wording), the swan's single way of flying, and the rescue.
Confirm Karna offers rewards to whoever shows him Arjuna, and that Shalya applies the fable to Karna as fed on the leavings of Dhritarashtra's sons.
Karna's reply includes harsh words about the Madra people; the script mentions only 'hard words' to avoid repeating regional insults.
